Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis:
The failing test `shouldThrowAnExceptionOnTruncatedEntries` expects an IOException to be thrown when reading a truncated tar archive. The test opens an input stream on a tar file and reads all entries, copying data to files. The test expects an exception on premature EOF, but currently no exception is thrown.

Looking at `TarArchiveInputStream.getNextTarEntry()`, the method reads entries sequentially. It skips remaining bytes of the current entry, then reads the next header block via `getRecord()`. If `getRecord()` returns null, indicating EOF, this method returns null as well.

The method `getRecord()` calls `readRecord()` to read one record (header block). `readRecord()` attempts to read a full block from input stream: it calls `IOUtils.readFully()` with the block size byte array. If fewer bytes than expected are read (indicating EOF in middle of block), it returns null.

`IOUtils.readFully()` tries to read the specified number of bytes, but returns the number of bytes actually read. It does not throw an IOException for premature EOF; it just returns a smaller count, which `readRecord()` interprets by returning null.

The problem is that in the scenario of a truncated tar file (premature EOF in the middle of a header record), `readRecord()` returns null, causing `getRecord()` to treat that as EOF (setting `hasHitEOF` flag). Consequently, `getNextTarEntry()` returns null, indicating no more entries. It silently stops without throwing an IOException as the test expects.

Hence, the root cause is that `TarArchiveInputStream.readRecord()` treats truncated records as normal EOF by returning null instead of throwing an IOException indicating corrupted or truncated file. This causes the input stream to silently stop instead of raising an error on unexpected EOF.

Recent bug reports mention silent finishes on unexpected EOF on tar streams, consistent with this diagnosis. The bug is likely in the handling of partial/short reads in `readRecord()` and cascading null returns indicating EOF rather than error.

Thus, the bug occurs because the method `readRecord()` treats truncated header record reads as normal EOF and returns null instead of throwing an exception. This causes `getNextTarEntry()` to silently finish instead of throwing IOException on truncated entries as expected by the test.

This explains why the test does not get an IOException and fails.

Next, candidates for fix are in `TarArchiveInputStream.readRecord()` and possibly `getRecord()`. The fix should detect truncated reads and throw IOException instead of returning null. The skipping of `readRecord()` returning null ultimately hides the truncation and should instead signal error.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
